claims.text: As-manufactured Q235 steel has a naturally formed, thin native Fe-oxide surface layer.
The native Fe-oxide film on untreated Q235 steel is an effective diffusion barrier under ambient conditions.
At room temperature, the intact native oxide limits oxidation and metal dissolution.
High-temperature molten-salt exposure causes phase transformations in the native oxide film.
Thermal-expansion mismatch and thermal stresses cause the native oxide film to crack or spall at 700–900 °C.
Accelerated chemical reactions in molten salt contribute to disruption of the native oxide film.
Disruption of the oxide film exposes the Q235 steel substrate.
Exposure of the substrate increases the rate of corrosive degradation.
Oxide-film thickness, uniformity, adhesion, and phase composition govern diffusion of oxidizing species.
Room-temperature salt exposure will produce minimal mass loss and a uniform, stable oxide morphology on untreated Q235 steel.
Untreated Q235 steel exposed to molten salt at 700–900 °C will exhibit significant mass loss.
High-temperature exposure will produce observable oxide spallation, cracking, or transformation to less-protective phases.
High-temperature exposure will produce localized corrosion features on untreated Q235 steel.
A thermally stabilized or thicker oxide film will provide better high-temperature protection than the untreated native film.
The proposed mechanism should govern only when salt chemistry and temperature are sufficiently aggressive to trigger thermally induced native-film failure.
The proposed mechanism should not apply when pre-oxidation or coating has modified the oxide chemistry or when salt aggressiveness is insufficient to cause spallation.
Matched untreated and oxide-stabilized Q235 specimens can be compared across room-temperature and 700–900 °C salt exposures to test the proposed mechanism.
Mass change, oxide morphology and composition, and electrochemical indicators can be measured to evaluate film failure and corrosion.
